summary: Mobility is near normal with an MF-Index of 71 and PT ridership at 1.24 million trips daily, but fuel‑saving outcomes remain far below theoretical expectations. High‑risk sectors such as retail, logistics and construction continue to drive mobility, suggesting targeted interventions are needed to sustain recovery and improve equity.

signals.detail: Theoretical fuel savings of 35.7 M L/week contrast sharply with the measured 334 k L saved in the first week of the WFH mandate, indicating compliance is only about 1% of the ceiling and the policy’s immediate impact is minimal.

Daily PT trips of 1.24 million are slightly below the pre‑pandemic daily average (~1.43 million), reflecting a ridership component of 72.7/100; recovery is evident but full normalization remains pending.

Retail & Services, Logistics and Construction exhibit low WFH adoption (15%, 8%, 5%) and high mobility scores (85‑95), signalling elevated exposure to congestion, emissions and labor‑productivity disruptions.

WFH uptake varies widely across sectors, with public & GLC employees at 60% versus under 10% in high‑risk industries, raising concerns that the current mandate benefits some workers disproportionately.

Fuel prices remain high (RON95 RM4.32/L, diesel RM5.07/L) and the fuel policy component scores 100, yet low realized fuel savings and only modest PT recovery suggest limited immediate modal shift away from private vehicles.

recommendation: Introduce sector‑specific incentives to raise WFH adoption in Retail, Logistics and Construction to at least 30% by Q2 2027, coupled with targeted subsidies for PT use and congestion pricing to accelerate modal shift and improve equity.
